newsitem.title: CHINA: China law aims to curb police abusing powers.
newsitem.headline: China law aims to curb police abusing powers.

text.p: China put into effect on Tuesday a law curbing the power of police to detain suspects without charge, but a dissident said the law would not stop authorities from hauling political activists into custody.
Six months of preparatory work for implementing the Law on Administrative Punishment found that some officials still resented and resisted the law, the Legal Daily newspaper said.

Other officials believed the new law was too troublesome to implement, and some thought that developing the economy was more important and that it did not matter if the law existed or not, the newspaper said.
The law, passed by parliament in March, bars police from holding a suspect for more than 30 days, after which public security officials must obtain an arrest warrant from a prosecutor.
Previously, suspects could be held without charge for months or even years.
"The Law on Administrative Punishment restricts the abuse of administration powers," the Legal Daily said.

Prominent dissident Liu Xiaobo welcomed the enactment of the law. "Better with a law than without a law," said Liu, who was detained by police without charges for eight months and released last January.
Under the new law, suspects can consult a lawyer after being interrogated by police. In the past, lawyers were allowed access to a case only shortly before trial.
Critics say the concept of rule by law remains alien to China, where imperial officials have wielded absolute power for centuries and their word alone was tantamount to law.
"Based on its political needs, the government will find other reasons to extend the detention of those holding different political views," Liu said in a telephone interview.

"It is an improvement but I feel...implementation could take some time," said Liu, one of four men who staged a hunger strike in Beijing's Tiananmen Square just days before the army brutally crushed student demonstrations for democracy in June 1989.
Administrative punishment has been one of the most powerful weapons of police against dissent.
The most prominent case of illegal detention is that of Wei Jingsheng, the father of China's struggling democracy movement.
Wei vanished for 20 months into police custody before being charged and sentenced last December to 14 years in prison for plotting to subvert the government.
Another case is that of student leader-turned-dissident Wang Dan, who remained in a security limbo on Tuesday.
Wang was detained in May 1995 in the run-up to the sixth anniversary of the June 1989 crackdown. Police have confirmed holding Wang but have yet to lodge formal charges against him.
Wang, a leader of the 1989 demonstrations, had served four years in prison for "counter-revolutionary" -- or subversive -- crimes.

Bao Tong, former secretary to Zhao Ziyang who was toppled as Communist Party chief after the 1989 demonstrations, was under effective house arrest despite completing his seven-year prison term last May.

Bao had been convicted of "counter-revolutionary incitement" and leaking state secrets -- believed to be related to the declaration of martial law in Beijing on May 20, 1989, of which student protesters had advanced warning.
